2-high safety look is dominant in the NFL; wondering about Leonhard
stories.summary:
I've gotten the sense that Leonhard is more of a single-high safety schemer than most, but that's just an impression. This piece in The Athletic explains why almost every team plays two-high now -- single-high is a route to disaster given today's QBs and WRs:  https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7488248/2026/08/06/two-high-safety-trend-nfl-defense/.



	 



	'After the Seattle Seahawks’ Legion of Boom-led era of single-high safety defenses paired with aggressive, attacking fronts, we saw an explosion in the passing game, punctuated by Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes throwing 50 touchdown passes in 2018. To combat the spike in passing production, defenses started playing more two-high coverages, meaning they kept two safeties deep before the snap to discourage deep passing. This top-down approach helped reduce explosive pass plays and forced offenses to drive the length of the field with more plays, making it harder to get into the end zone.



	Offenses have loaded up on bigger bodies this offseason and seem to be gearing up to focus more on the running game, but can they force defenses to cycle back into putting a safety in the box? After speaking with defensive coaches, the collective answer was, surprisingly, no. Two-high defenses are here to stay. Quarterbacks and receivers are simply too good. 



	...



	Two-high coverages aren’t immune to deep passes. There are still weaknesses in any coverage, but it makes them harder to find. The top quarterbacks can decipher these coverages after the snap, find the weaknesses and hit deep passes with anticipation, but two-high makes it much more difficult to execute.



	Committing to this style of defense means you have to be comfortable playing with a light box. Even though a defense can rotate into a single-high coverage, the safety is coming from depth and he’s not an immediate part of the run fit. Defenses have to be OK giving up efficient runs on the ground. The theory is that it is very difficult to keep stringing together efficient runs, and offensive coordinators will eventually get impatient.



	“If you’re giving up a bunch of explosive runs, obviously you’re going to have to do something, but if they’re getting four or five yards of pop because you’re in split safety and they’re patient enough to do it, I can live with that sometimes,” an AFC defensive play caller said. “I know that it’s not sexy, but the second you go single-high, the explosive passing rate goes ridiculously high.”



	...



	“If you look at an explosive play as a 15-plus-yard play, whether it’s a run or pass, the percentage of the offense scoring a touchdown if they get an explosive versus the percentage if you don’t give up an explosive is much higher. The likeliness of the offense scoring a touchdown without an explosive is very low,” an NFC defensive coordinator said. “Ninety percent of explosives come from passes. So as long as you don’t give up an explosive, they’re likely not gonna give up a touchdown.”



	From 2022 to 2025, offenses scored touchdowns on 42.7 percent of drives in which they had at least one play of 15 yards or more. On drives when they didn’t have an explosive, that percentage dropped to 21.8 percent.



	It’s much easier to create an explosive through the passing game than on the ground. Though it’s easier to get efficient runs against two-high, the scheme actually does a better job of containing explosive runs. Big runs happen when defenses crowd the line of scrimmage and the ball carrier gets through the second level. By putting a safety back, the defense strengthens its second-level line of defense, and defensive backs are becoming better at fitting the run and tackling from depth.



	“The pace of our fits from depth has gotten better,” an NFC defensive coach said.



	The combination of more repetitions defending the run and an emphasis from scouts on finding good tacklers has improved open-field tackling. In this style of defense, coaches talked about the need to remain disciplined even when teams are having success running the ball. You can’t abandon your defensive philosophy, and if a team is really dominating on the ground, there are schematic levers to pull to try to disrupt the run game.



	“When you’re in nickel (five defensive backs) and split-safety coverages versus 12 and 13 personnel (multiple tight ends), you’re gonna give us some 7- and 8-yard runs, and that’s where you got to be comfortable doing that and have the discipline to stay with it,” an AFC head coach said. “Then you have got to have the ability to call a run blitz or do something to kind of get them off schedule. And now, you don’t have the deck in your favor.”



	A defense can give up several efficient runs in a row, but if a defensive play caller can create a negative through blitzing or changing the front to confuse the blocking scheme, the defense can get the offense into second-and-long, and then it is right back on track. By scouting and looking at the analytics, defensive coaches can help their light fronts gain an advantage with their calls.'

stories.title: The Athletic QB Tiers (2 Panelists Voted Josh as Tier 2)
stories.summary:
The annual Athletic QB Tiers came out this morning.  Unbelievably, 2 panelists voted Josh as a tier 2 QB!  These 2 panelists must be incredibly spiteful or astonishingly stupid.  How do you not immediately dismiss any contributors to your story that claim Allen is not in the top tier of QBs in the NFL?!  I know it is a paywall article, but here is the link.  https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/interactive/nfl-quarterback-tiers-insider-rankings-2026/ 



	 



	How panelists voted in 2026



	Tier 1  - 48 votes



	Tier 2 - 2



	 



	Allen moved one vote closer toward unanimous Tier 1 status and could be the most feared quarterback in the league.



	“Josh Allen is unreal,” a defensive coordinator said. “He and Stafford are the two guys I would not want to play the most. Allen’s ability to make plays, be hard to tackle, put the team on his shoulders — when it’s fourth down, he is going to win.”



	 



	One veteran coach said Allen still has much to learn.



	“Josh Allen, with under 30 seconds left in the half, runs for a meaningless 12-yard gain and fumbles and gives up a field goal in a playoff game to go behind two scores against Denver,” this coach said. “Until he quits doing that, you can’t rank him as the top quarterback. That is one of the worst plays I’ve ever seen. Cost them the game.”



	 



	Others saw the positives.



	“The thing that jumped out to me about the playoffs last year was the physicality and the plays the quarterbacks make with their toughness, their size and their strength, particularly as they advance on,” an exec said. “Josh has got that. Obviously, it’s TBD with (new coach) Joe Brady, but one thing that those guys in the top tier do is, when you get off the bus on the road, the other 52 guys think they got a chance.”



	Allen led all quarterbacks in rushing yards (579) and rushing touchdowns (14) in 2025.



	 



	“He’s the real deal because he can do it as a dropback quarterback, and they do some run game with him,” another defensive coordinator said. “The way they use him is the way Baltimore has to use Lamar (Jackson) to get the most out of him.”



	A GM noted that the Bills have given Allen a strong defense and a strong run game, but not at the same time.



	“Josh is a 1 because he is the reason they remain competitive,” this GM said. “He’s so physically talented. But I’m ready to say he’s never gonna win a Super Bowl because their team’s getting worse around him, and I think his style of football is going to start breaking him down physically.”

stories.title: CJGJ = Problem Child?
stories.summary:
As many of you have, I have been tuned into the offseason/Training Camp and I have to be honest, I am seeing something brewing that makes me feel uneasy.  It's CJ Gardner-Johnson.  When they first signed him, I was like ok, they got a dawg style guy with some talent.  Hey we need some dawgs and this could help our defense.  However, after seeing the constant sh***t talking and now this whole streaming "thing" with Brady and then going live after to talk about it.  It's clear to me this guy just doesn't get it.  Almost like some Antonio Brown vibes.  He has had issues with his former teams.  Quite a few teams I might add. 



	 



	There was a certain culture developed here over the past 8-9 years. You heard Jim Leonhard reference it in his presser regarding the level of professionalism that is displayed by the players.  I fully understand if it gets out of control they can just cut him, but I hope this guy doesn't kill the vibes and make training camp unenjoyable for everyone. This can have a ripple effect throughout the team.  He appears to be the exact type of player (attitude and maturity) we have tried to avoid over the last 9 years.

stories.title: Bruins hire former Sabres GM Kevyn Adams as senior advisor
stories.summary:
Former Buffalo Sabres general manager Kevyn Adams is back in the NHL.
The Boston Bruins on Tuesday named Adams, 51, a senior advisor to GM Don Sweeney.
The Sabres fired Adams on Dec. 15, almost halfway through his sixth season as GM, and replaced him with Jarmo Kekalainen, who had been serving as a senior advisor.

stories.title: Sabres bring in John Davidson as senior advisor; Buffalo makes minor trade
stories.summary:
The Buffalo Sabres have added to their front office by hiring John Davidson, a popular former goalie and broadcaster who has spent most of the past 20 years working as a president of hockey operations, as a senior advisor, the team announced Monday.
